newsitem.title: CHINA: Malaysia tells China, U.S. to make love, not war.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia tells China, U.S. to make love, not war.

text.p: China and the United States should learn to work together -- like elephants making love in the jungle -- to ensure stability in the Asia-Pacific region, Malaysia's foreign minister said on Thursday.

Any conflict between Washington and Beijing could threaten the welfare of the booming "Asian tiger" nations of Southeast Asia, Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told a forum on international relations in the Chinese capital.
"China-U.S. relations will be a major determinant for peace and stability in the region," he said in a speech on Beijing's role in the Asian-Pacific area.

"I like to see China and (the) U.S. as two elephants... when they are hungry or angry the jungle is no longer a safe place even for tigers," he said. "Let us hope they will make love: then only the bushes will be trampled."

Abdullah Ahmad said he was encouraged that Beijing and Washington were continuing efforts to improve their troubled relationship, often tested by disputes over issues ranging from Taiwan to human rights to trade.

Malaysia believed Beijing's leaders when they said China would not practice hegemony or power politics, even after their nation had completed its almost inevitable transformation into a regional "mega-power", the foreign minister said.
Beijing's relations with its neighbours, including members of the seven-country Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), would be a test of Chinese goodwill, he said.
"What is important today is to see China as a friend and potential partner," he told an audience of Chinese officials, scholars and Asian diplomats.

East Asians should not be concerned by Western journalists and writers who said China was a threat, that future Sino-U.S. conflict was inevitable or that East Asia's economic miracle was ending, he said.
"They play the role of the prophet of doom for us," he said. "We need not be over-worried by these reports and predictions in the Western media."
Political will was needed to resolve disputes involving the South China Sea, where a number of ASEAN nations and China have overlapping territorial claims, he said.

Beijing says almost the entire sea, including the resource-rich Spratly Islands, historically belongs to China and has provoked regional concerns in recent months by sending research ships to the area.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Malaysia, Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philipines and Brunei.
